concepts.name: The speed relationship
concepts.description: Distance, speed and time are locked together by one equation.

concepts.name: Unit conversion
concepts.description: Moving between km/hr and m/s without losing a factor.

concepts.name: Average speed
concepts.description: Total distance over total time — never the average of the speeds.

concepts.name: Relative speed
concepts.description: Speeds add when approaching and subtract when chasing.

concepts.name: Late and early problems
concepts.description: Journeys compared at two different speeds.

concepts.name: Circular tracks
concepts.description: Runners going opposite ways close the gap at the sum of their speeds; going the same way, at the difference. They are all at the start together after the LCM of their lap times.

concepts.name: Meeting points and multi-stage journeys
concepts.description: Two movers heading towards each other close the gap at the sum of their speeds. For journeys in stages, add up the distances and the times (including stops) before dividing.

formulas.title: Speed, distance and time
formulas.prompt: What is the relationship between speed, distance and time?
formulas.formula:
Speed = Distance ÷ Time
Distance = Speed × Time
Time = Distance ÷ Speed
formulas.explanation: One relationship in three arrangements. Keep all three units consistent before substituting.
formulas.commonMistake: Mixing units — minutes with km/hr, or metres with hours.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A car covers 120 km in 2 hours. Which formula gives its speed?

formulas.title: km/hr to m/s
formulas.prompt: How do you convert between km/hr and m/s?
formulas.formula:
km/hr → m/s : multiply by 5/18
m/s → km/hr : multiply by 18/5
formulas.explanation: 1 km/hr = 1000 m per 3600 s = 5/18 m/s. Train and short-distance questions almost always need this.
formulas.commonMistake: Using 18/5 when converting into m/s, which makes the speed far too large.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A train travels at 72 km/hr and you need its speed in m/s. What do you multiply by?

formulas.title: Average speed
formulas.prompt: How do you find average speed over a journey?
formulas.formula:
Average speed = Total distance ÷ Total time
For equal distances at x and y: 2xy ÷ (x + y)
formulas.explanation: More time is spent at the slower speed, so the average always sits below the midpoint of the two speeds.
formulas.example:
40 km/hr out, 60 km/hr back
= (2 × 40 × 60) ÷ 100
= 48 km/hr, not 50
formulas.applicationPrompt: A car goes at 40 km/hr and returns at 60 km/hr. Which formula gives the average speed?

formulas.title: Relative speed
formulas.prompt: Two objects move. How fast does the gap between them change?
formulas.formula:
Opposite directions: add the speeds
Same direction: subtract the speeds
formulas.explanation: Convert a two-object problem into a one-object problem by working with the gap and the relative speed.
formulas.example:
Two trains 100 km apart approach at 60 and 40 km/hr
Relative speed = 100 km/hr
They meet after 100 ÷ 100 = 1 hour
formulas.commonMistake: Adding speeds for a chase, which should subtract.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Two cars approach each other at 60 and 40 km/hr. What speed closes the gap?

formulas.title: Late and early journeys
formulas.prompt: The same journey at two speeds arrives late and early. How do you find the distance?
formulas.explanation: The time difference is the late minutes plus the early minutes, converted into hours.
formulas.example:
At 5 km/hr 10 min late, at 6 km/hr 5 min early
Difference = 15 min = 1/4 hr
d/5 − d/6 = 1/4 → d = 7.5 km
formulas.commonMistake: Using only the late time or only the early time as the difference.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Walking at 5 km/hr you are 10 minutes late; at 6 km/hr you are 5 minutes early. How do you find the distance?

formulas.title: Meeting on a circular track
formulas.prompt: When do two runners on a circular track meet?
formulas.formula: Opposite directions: L ÷ (a + b); same direction: L ÷ (a − b); all at the start again: LCM of the lap times
formulas.explanation: L is the track length. Meeting means together they have covered one lap more (same direction) or one lap between them (opposite).
formulas.example: L = 600 m at 5 and 7 m/s: opposite → 600 ÷ 12 = 50 s; same → 600 ÷ 2 = 300 s
formulas.commonMistake: Using the sum of the speeds when they run the same way.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Two runners on a 600 m track run at 5 m/s and 7 m/s in opposite directions. When do they first meet?

formulas.title: Meeting point
formulas.prompt: Where do two movers heading towards each other meet?
formulas.formula: Time to meet = D ÷ (a + b); A covers a × that time. After meeting: (a ÷ b)² = B's time after meeting ÷ A's time after meeting
formulas.explanation: The second relation uses the times each takes, after meeting, to reach the other's starting point.
formulas.example: D = 300 km at 60 and 90 km/h: they meet after 2 h, 120 km from A
formulas.commonMistake: Splitting the distance equally instead of in the ratio of the speeds.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Two trains 300 km apart travel towards each other at 60 and 90 km/h. How far from the first train's start do they meet?

formulas.title: A fraction of the usual speed
formulas.prompt: Travelling at a/b of the usual speed makes someone late (or early) by t. What is the usual time?
formulas.formula:
New time = b/a of the usual time
Usual time = t ÷ |b/a − 1|
formulas.explanation: For a fixed distance, time is inversely proportional to speed.
formulas.example: At 3/4 of the usual speed, 20 minutes late: the time becomes 4/3, so 1/3 of the usual time is 20 minutes and the usual time is 60 minutes.
formulas.commonMistake: Taking 3/4 of the time instead of 4/3.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Walking at 5/6 of his usual speed, a man is 10 minutes late.

formulas.title: Late at one speed, early at another
formulas.prompt: At speed s₁ you arrive late and at s₂ you arrive early. What is the distance?
formulas.formula: Distance = s₁ × s₂ × (total time gap) ÷ (s₂ − s₁)
formulas.explanation: It is d/s₁ − d/s₂ = gap, already solved for d. Add the late and early times to get the gap, in hours.
formulas.example: 4 km/h is 10 minutes late, 5 km/h is 5 minutes early: gap 15 minutes = 1/4 hour, so d = 4 × 5 × 1/4 ÷ 1 = 5 km.
formulas.commonMistake: Subtracting the late and early minutes instead of adding them, or leaving the gap in minutes.
formulas.applicationPrompt: At 30 km/h a rider is 6 minutes late; at 40 km/h, 3 minutes early.

formulas.title: Speeds worth knowing by heart
formulas.prompt: Which km/h speeds convert to whole metres per second?
formulas.explanation: Each 18 km/h is 5 m/s, so multiples of 18 convert cleanly.
formulas.commonMistake: Multiplying by 18/5 when going from km/h to m/s. The m/s number is always the smaller one.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A train runs at 54 km/h. How many metres does it cover in 12 seconds?

formulas.title: Stoppage time per hour
formulas.prompt: A bus averages one speed without stops and a lower one with stops. How long does it stop each hour?
formulas.formula: Stoppage per hour = (Speed without stops − Speed with stops) ÷ Speed without stops × 60 minutes
formulas.explanation: The distance lost in an hour would have taken that long to cover at the running speed.
formulas.example: 60 km/h without stops, 45 km/h with: 15 ÷ 60 × 60 = 15 minutes per hour.
formulas.commonMistake: Dividing by the speed with stops.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A train does 80 km/h excluding halts and 64 km/h including them.

levels.title: One Relationship, Three Forms
levels.description: The speed equation, and the unit discipline that makes it reliable.

blocks.title: Everything comes from one equation
blocks.body: Distance = Speed × Time. Rearranged, it gives speed and time as well. There is no second formula to learn in this topic — only situations to translate.

blocks.title: The unit rule
blocks.caption: Check units before substituting, every single time.

blocks.body: Most lost marks here are unit errors, not method errors. If the distance is in metres and the speed in km/hr, the answer is wrong before you start.

blocks.title: Average speed is not the average of speeds
blocks.body:
Travel out at 40 km/hr and back at 60 km/hr, and the average is 48 km/hr — not 50. You spend more time at the slower speed, so it carries more weight.

Always go back to total distance ÷ total time.

levels.title: Motion Formulas
levels.description: The speed relationship, conversions, average speed and relative speed.

levels.title: Direct Motion Questions
levels.description: Single-step speed, time and conversion problems.

levels.title: Average and Relative Speed
levels.description: Round trips, approaching objects and trains crossing poles.

levels.title: Advanced: Circular Tracks and Meeting Points
levels.description: Runners on circular tracks, meeting points, and journeys in stages.

blocks.title: Round and round
blocks.body: On a circular track the gap between two runners is at most one lap. Running opposite ways, they close it at the sum of their speeds; running the same way, only at the difference.

blocks.title: Heading towards each other
blocks.caption: The meeting point splits the distance in the ratio of the speeds.

blocks.body: For an average over several stages, never average the speeds. Add the total distance and the total time, including any stops.

levels.title: Challenge: Circular Tracks and Meeting Points
levels.description: Laps and overtaking, meeting points, speed ratios and multi-stage averages.

questions.question: A car covers 120 km in 2 hours. What is its speed?

hints.text: How far does the car travel in one hour?

questions.question: Convert 72 km/hr into metres per second.
solutionSteps: To go from km/hr to m/s, multiply by 5/18.

hints.text: m/s values are smaller than the km/hr value.
Multiply by 5 and divide by 18.

questions.question: How many hours does a cyclist take to cover 45 km at 15 km/hr?

hints.text: The cyclist covers 15 km each hour.

questions.question: A train covers a distance d in time t. Which expression gives its speed?
questions.explanation: Speed measures distance covered per unit of time, so the distance is divided by the time.
questions.method: Read the unit: km per hour means km ÷ hours.

hints.text: Look at the units: km/hr literally means km divided by hours.

questions.question: A car travels to a town at 40 km/hr and returns along the same road at 60 km/hr. Its average speed for the whole trip is 50 km/hr.
questions.explanation: The average is 2 × 40 × 60 ÷ 100 = 48 km/hr. More time is spent at the slower speed, so the average is pulled below 50.
solutionSteps: Take the one-way distance as 120 km.
Out: 3 hours. Back: 2 hours. Total 240 km in 5 hours.

hints.text: Which leg of the journey takes longer?
Pick a convenient distance such as 120 km and compute both times.

questions.question: A man walks to work at 40 km/hr and returns by the same route at 60 km/hr. What is his average speed for the round trip?
questions.explanation: For equal distances, average = 2xy/(x + y) = (2 × 40 × 60) ÷ 100 = 48 km/hr.
solutionSteps: The distances are equal, so use 2xy ÷ (x + y).

hints.text: The answer must be below 50 — more time is spent at 40 km/hr.
Use 2xy ÷ (x + y).

questions.question: Two trains 100 km apart move towards each other at 60 km/hr and 40 km/hr. After how long do they meet?
questions.explanation: Approaching trains close the gap at 60 + 40 = 100 km/hr, so 100 km takes 1 hour.
questions.method: Add speeds when moving towards each other.

hints.text: How fast is the gap between them shrinking?
Both trains contribute, so the speeds add.

questions.question: A train 150 metres long crosses a pole in 9 seconds. What is its speed in km/hr?
questions.explanation: Crossing a pole means covering its own length: 150 ÷ 9 = 16.67 m/s, and 16.67 × 18/5 = 60 km/hr.
solutionSteps: Crossing a pole means travelling the train's own length: 150 m.
questions.method: Distance is the train's length; convert m/s to km/hr at the end.

hints.text: What distance does the train actually cover to pass a pole?
Its own length, 150 m.
Convert m/s to km/hr by multiplying by 18/5.

questions.question: Walking at 5 km/hr a man reaches his office 10 minutes late; at 6 km/hr he arrives 5 minutes early. How far is his office?
questions.explanation: The time difference is 15 minutes = 1/4 hour, so d/5 − d/6 = 1/4, giving d/30 = 1/4 and d = 7.5 km.
solutionSteps: Total time difference = 10 late + 5 early = 15 minutes = 1/4 hour.
questions.method: The gap between the two journey times equals late + early.

hints.text: How much sooner does the faster walk arrive, in total?
10 minutes late to 5 minutes early is a 15-minute swing.
Write both times as d/5 and d/6 and subtract.

commonMistakes: Using 10 or 5 minutes alone as the time difference.

questions.question: A car covers the first 60 km of a journey at 30 km/hr and the next 60 km at 60 km/hr. What is its average speed for the whole journey?
questions.explanation: Times are 2 hours and 1 hour, so 120 km in 3 hours gives 40 km/hr.

hints.text: Work out the time for each leg separately.
The slow leg takes twice as long, so it dominates.

questions.question: Two runners start together from the same point on a 600 m circular track and run in opposite directions at 5 m/s and 7 m/s. After how many seconds do they first meet?
questions.explanation: Running opposite ways, they close the lap at 5 + 7 = 12 m/s, so they meet after 600 ÷ 12 = 50 s.

hints.text: Together they need to cover one full lap.
Add the two speeds.

commonMistakes: Using the difference of the speeds, giving 300 s.

questions.question: Two towns are 300 km apart. A train leaves each town at the same time, heading towards the other, at 60 km/h and 90 km/h. How far from the slower train's town do they meet?
questions.explanation: They close the gap at 150 km/h and meet after 300 ÷ 150 = 2 h. The slower train has gone 60 × 2 = 120 km.
questions.method: Find the meeting time first, then one train's distance.

hints.text: How fast is the gap closing?
Multiply that time by the slower speed.

commonMistakes: Splitting the distance equally, giving 150 km.

questions.question: Two runners start together from the same point on a 600 m circular track and run in the same direction at 5 m/s and 7 m/s. After how many seconds does the faster runner first lap the slower one?
questions.explanation: Running the same way, the gap grows at 7 − 5 = 2 m/s. Lapping means gaining a full 600 m: 600 ÷ 2 = 300 s.

hints.text: To lap someone you must gain one full lap on them.
Use the difference of the speeds.

questions.question: Two runners take 40 seconds and 60 seconds to complete a lap of a circular track. If they start together from the starting point, after how many seconds are they next at the starting point together?
questions.explanation: The first is at the start every 40 s and the second every 60 s. They coincide first at LCM(40, 60) = 120 s.
solutionSteps: Start times: multiples of 40 and of 60.
questions.method: Both at the start together: LCM of the lap times.

hints.text: When is each runner back at the start?
Find the first time common to both lists.

questions.question: Two trains start at the same time from P and Q, heading towards each other. After they meet, the train from P takes 4 hours to reach Q and the train from Q takes 9 hours to reach P. What is the ratio of the speed of the train from P to the speed of the train from Q?
questions.explanation: For two movers after meeting, (speed₁ ÷ speed₂)² = t₂ ÷ t₁ = 9 ÷ 4, so the ratio is √(9/4) = 3 : 2.
questions.method: Use the square-root relation between speeds and post-meeting times.

hints.text: The faster train takes less time after the meeting.
The speed ratio is the square root of the time ratio, flipped.

questions.question: A car covers the first 150 km of a journey at 50 km/h and the next 150 km at 75 km/h, with a 1-hour stop in between. What is its average speed for the whole journey, including the stop?
questions.explanation: Times: 150 ÷ 50 = 3 h and 150 ÷ 75 = 2 h, plus the 1 h stop: 6 h in all. Average = 300 ÷ 6 = 50 km/h.
solutionSteps: Stage 1: 3 h; stage 2: 2 h; stop: 1 h.
questions.method: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.

hints.text: Find the time for each stage.
Do not forget the stop.

commonMistakes: Leaving out the stop, giving 60 km/h.

questions.question: Three runners take 24 s, 36 s and 40 s to complete a lap of a circular track. They start together from the starting point. After how many seconds are all three at the starting point together again?
questions.method: All at the start together: the LCM of every lap time.

hints.text: Write each lap time as a product of primes.
Take the highest power of each prime.
